## PAGE 14

### Content: Continuation of Section F (Paired Permutation Test) and Section G (Cross-Architecture Analysis)

**Table 7: Paired permutation test for compound severity: importance vs. random eviction on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B (s=0.9 profiling subset, 10,000 permutations, Bonferroni-corrected).** The table states: "The monotonic Δ pattern is confirmed at n=496 (Table 1)."

Table 7 data:

| s | Observed Δ̄ | 95% CI | p_boot |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.15 | 0.97 | [0.19, 0.62] | 0.0012 |
| 0.20 | 1.97 | [0.61, 1.67] | <0.001 |
| 0.25 | 3.34 | [1.06, 6.64] | <0.001 |
| 0.30 | 9.85 | [6.71, 10.25] | <0.001 |

Key text: "Per-problem distributions of the paired severity difference Δ_s = H_imp,s − H_rand,s under importance-based eviction are right-skewed at all sparsity levels, with mean/median ratios ranging from 1.2× (s=0.15) to 1.6× (s=0.30) for DeepSeek and 1.1× to 1.4× for Qwen."

"The permutation null distributions are approximately symmetric around zero at all sparsity levels. At s=0.15, the observed statistic falls at the 99.93th percentile of the null (p_boot = 0.0012); at s ≥ 0.20, no permutation exceeds the observed statistic."

"Table 7 reports the results. All four sparsity levels reject H₀ after Bonferroni correction (p_boot < 0.005), with observed median differences increasing monotonically from 0.37 at s=0.15 to 8.5 at s=0.30."

"The monotonic growth of both the point estimate and the CI lower bound (0.19 → 0.69 → 1.66 → 6.70) confirms that compound severity amplification strengthens with sparsity—not merely in central tendency but also in worst-case lower bounds."

**Figure 4: Forest plot of permutation test results.** Horizontal bars show 95% permutation CIs; diamonds mark observed median differences Δ̄. All CIs lie entirely above zero, confirming significant strategy-dependent severity at every sparsity level. The plot shows four rows for s=0.15, s=0.20, s=0.25, s=0.30, with median diff on the x-axis (0 to ~15).

Key claims from surrounding text:

"The median paired difference increases monotonically (Δ̄: 0.023 → 0.256), consistent with a genuine but weak trend—partially confirming the cross-architecture hypothesis while uncovering the substantially weaker interaction on LlamaForCausalLM."

"The absolute magnitude is architecture-dependent: LLaMA severity differences are ~40× smaller than DeepSeek and ~7× smaller than Qwen."

"Notably, random eviction on LLaMA also exhibits a non-trivial phase gradient (0.15 → 0.43), substantially reducing the strategy contrast that is the hallmark of the phase-strategy interaction on Qwen2 models."

### Section G: Cross-Architecture Analysis

"To test whether the phase-modulated severity pattern extends beyond the Qwen2 architecture, we replicate the experiment on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B (LlamaForCausalLM, 8B parameters; n=49 paired problems). Table 8 reports the strategy-dependent severity comparison across sparsity levels."

"The evidence for a strategy contrast on LLaMA is mixed: at s=0.15, the bootstrap CI excludes zero (0.002, 0.043) but the Bonferroni-corrected Wilcoxon test is non-significant (p_Wilcox=0.219); conversely, at s=0.30 the CI spans zero ([-0.069, 0.54]) while the Wilcoxon test reaches significance (p_Wilcox=0.029). At intermediate levels (s ∈ {0.20, 0.25}), neither CI nor Wilcoxon..."

**Post-hoc power analysis:** "We computed post-hoc power via bootstrap simulation (B=10,000) to assess what claims the n=49 sample can and cannot support. For the within-importance phase..."

"The CW/Wilcoxon discrepancy reflects differing power profiles under small n with heavy-tailed distributions: the percentile bootstrap CI is based on the resampled median distribution and is less sensitive to tail observations, while the Wilcoxon signed rank test uses signed ranks and is more sensitive to tail outliers. This inconsistency itself supports the conservative 'mixed/weak evidence' interpretation."

---

## PAGE 15

### Table 8: Cross architecture validation on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B (LlamaForCausalLM).

Table header: "Δ̄: median paired difference (importance − random) with bootstrap 95% CI (P=10,000). p: Bonferroni-corrected Wilcoxon signed-rank p (k=8). n=49 paired problems."

Table 8 data:

| s | Δ̄ | [95% CI] | p_boot |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.15 | 0.020 | [0.002, 0.043] | 0.219 |
| 0.20 | 0.027 | [-0.003, 0.047] | 0.273 |
| 0.25 | 0.095 | [-0.001, 0.301] | 0.063 |
| 0.30 | 0.206 | [-0.069, 0.544] | **0.029** |

Key text: "gradient testing Δ̄_imp > 0, power exceeds 0.99 at all four sparsity levels, confirming that the sample is sufficient to detect the importance-based severity gradient. For strategy comparison testing Δ̄_imp − Δ̄_rand > 0, power ranges from 0.26 (s=0.15) to 0.63 (s=0.30), indicating that the sample is underpowered for detecting strategy-level differences at their observed effect sizes. Extrapolating from the observed effect sizes and variances, n ≥ 200 paired problems would be needed to achieve 0.80 power for the strategy comparison at s=0.30."

"This motivates the conservative interpretation in §5.5: the within-importance gradient is confirmed, but the strategy×phase interaction requires larger-scale replication."

### Section H: Analysis: Entropy-Discrimination Collapse

#### H.1 Discrimination Collapse

"Head pruning reduces the number of heads contributing to cumulative importance scores, flattening the score distribution. Table 9 quantifies this effect: the Gini coefficient decreases by 0.030–0.081 (DeepSeek) and 0.010–0.020 (Qwen) after pruning, with consistent negative deltas across all 16 conditions (both models × 4 sparsity levels × 2 strategies). The CV delta is likewise negative in all 8 importance-based conditions. The same pattern holds under random eviction, confirming that discrimination collapse is a consequence of head pruning per se, not of the eviction strategy."

"When importance scores lose discriminability, thresholding degenerates into a noise-sensitive selection—functionally approaching biased random eviction. This is phase-dependent: in low-sparsity phases, attention is already broadly distributed, so pruning-induced flattening has maximum impact; in high-sparsity phases, concentration is preserved. Random eviction is immune because its decisions are independent of score quality,"

**Table 9: Discrimination collapse under importance-based eviction. ΔGini and ΔCV are post-pruning minus baseline; negative values indicate reduced discriminative power.**

Table 9 data:

| Model | s | ΔGini | ΔCV |
|---|---|---|---|
| DeepSeek | 0.15 | −0.030 | −0.56 |
| DeepSeek | 0.20 | −0.040 | −0.77 |
| DeepSeek | 0.25 | −0.065 | −1.20 |
| DeepSeek | 0.30 | −0.081 | −1.66 |
| Qwen | 0.15 | −0.010 | −0.05 |
| Qwen | 0.20 | −0.012 | −0.21 |
| Qwen | 0.25 | −0.015 | −0.43 |
| Qwen | 0.30 | −0.020 | −1.14 |

#### H.2 Entropy Redistribution

"Beyond discrimination collapse, we examine whether head pruning also redistributes the attention entropy of surviving heads. We measure the mean attention entropy per head:"

**Equation (7):**

$$N_l^{(s)} = -\sum_j \alpha_{l,j}^{(s)} \log \alpha_{l,j}^{(s)}$$

"and compute ΔN as change from baseline (no pruning) to the pruned condition."

"For DeepSeek under importance-based eviction, the entropy delta is consistently negative across all four sparsity levels (ΔN ∈ [−0.047, −0.080]; Table 10), indicating that importance-based pruning systematically selects heads whose removal concentrates attention in the surviving heads, reinforcing discrimination collapse."

"For Qwen, the entropy pattern only partially replicates. The delta is negative at s=0.15 (1.42%) and s=0.30 (s=0.071 (s=0.076), consistent with DeepSeek. However, at s=0.25, the delta reverses to +0.015, with 22 of 30 problems showing positive entropy change. At s=0.25 the reversal is near zero (−0.007). The s=0.25 reversal is systematic rather than a statistical artifact: it is consistent across all three reasoning phases (Qwen: +0.032, mid: +0.031, high: +0.017). We interpret this as a genuine model-specific difference, possibly arising from distinct head specialization patterns: Qwen's instruction tuning (vs. DeepSeek's distillation-based training) may produce head configurations where removing 25% of heads triggers compensatory broadening rather than concentration."

### Section I: Discrimination Collapse Details

"This cross-model consistency (Table 9) establishes discrimination collapse as a robust consequence of compound sparsity. When importance scores lose discriminative power, thresholding the bottom-s fraction becomes noise-sensitive: small perturbations change which positions cross the eviction boundary. In the limit of perfectly uniform scores, importance-based eviction degenerates into an arbitrary selection functionally equivalent to biased random eviction. The same pattern holds under random eviction (DeepSeek: −0.031 to −0.071; Qwen: −0.019 to −0.046), confirming that discrimination collapse is a consequence of head pruning per se, not of the eviction strategy."

### Section J: Extended Discussion

"On the predictability of phase-modulated severity. The compound interaction is not uniformly fragile—it is selectively fragile in a phase-dependent manner (H_imp: 0.10 at s ≤ 0.30)."

"**Random masking as falsification control.** At n=500, random eviction develops a detectable but weak phase gradient above s ≈ 0.20; non-significant at s < 0.20 for both models, but significant at s ≥ 0.25 (DS: Δ=0.26–0.51, p_boot < 10^-15; QW: Δ=0.39–0.91, p_boot < 10^-15). Where significant, the random phase gradient is 3–20× weaker than importance-based, confirming that the dominant amplification is strategy-specific."

"**Entropy mechanism boundary conditions.** Directly measuring per-head entropy shifts across ar-"

"chitecturally distinct models—and identifying what training-time properties determine whether entropy concentrates or disperses under head pruning—would clarify the boundary conditions of the full mechanism."

### Section K: Extended Limitations

"**Model scale.** All experiments are conducted at the 7B parameter scale. Whether the phase-modulated severity patterns persist, amplify, or attenuate at larger scales (e.g., 70B) remains untested. Larger models may exhibit different attention redundancy structures that alter the discrimination collapse dynamics (and the model-dependent entropy pattern) may behave differently at scale."

"**Architectural scope.** Our two models—DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct—share the Qwen2ForCausalLM architecture. The cross-model replication (§5.5) establishes that the findings are not artifacts of a single model's weights, though both models share the same Qwen2ForCausalLM architecture. Preliminary cross-architecture validation on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B (LlamaForCausalLM, §5.5, Appendix G) shows qualitatively consistent within-importance phase gradients (d_s ≈ 1.0) but a substantially weaker strategy × phase interaction than in Qwen2-based architectures; random pruning also exhibits a non-trivial phase gradient on LLaMA, reducing the strategy contrast. This partial confirmation (s=0.20 Wilcoxon p_adj=0.029, s=0.25 non-significant) suggests the qualitative pattern may generalize but quantitative impact is architecture-dependent. Comprehensive cross-architecture validation across more diverse designs (e.g., Mistral, multi-latent attention architecture) and scales remains an important next step."

"**Task coverage.** We evaluate exclusively on MATH-500, a mathematical reasoning benchmark. Different reasoning tasks—code generation, commonsense reasoning, multi-hop question answering—may induce different phase structures with different sparsity distributions, potentially altering the severity gradient profile. Generalizing the phase-strategy interaction to broader reasoning domains is an important next step."

"**Statistical scope.** Bootstrap confidence intervals use B=10,000 resamples (seed=42). The primary analysis uses n=496 paired problems for..."

---

## PAGE 17

### Continuation of Section K (Extended Limitations)

"DeepSeek (4 excluded) and n=475 for Qwen (25 excluded); the permutation test (Table 7) uses n=49 from an initial profiling subset. The severity difference distribution is right-skewed (mean/median ratios up to 10.1), motivating our use of medians and nonparametric tests rather than parametric alternatives. All four profiling-subset permutation tests reject H₀ after Bonferroni correction (p_boot < 0.005; Table 7), with CI lower bounds increasing from 0.19 to 6.70—confirming the effect direction at every sparsity level. At n=196, Wilcoxon signed-rank tests confirm all conditions with p_boot < 10^-14 (Table 3). The permutation CIs at higher sparsity are wider at s=0.30 ([6.70, 16.25] at s=0.30), reflecting genuine variance in per-problem severity amplification."

"At s=0.60, random eviction on both models becomes significant ≈ 0.25 (QWen: Δ=0.39, p_boot < 10^-15 at s=0.30; bootstrapping CI excludes zero). These effects are genuine but 2.7–20× weaker than importance-based eviction at the same sparsity levels, consistent with a weak phase gradient that is detectable at sufficient sample size but not the primary driver of compound severity."

"**Sparsity range.** Our experiments span s ∈ {0.15, 0.20, 0.25, 0.30}, a moderate range representative of practical deployment targets. More extreme sparsity (s > 0.50) may exhibit qualitatively different interaction dynamics—the subexponential growth pattern suggests the severity gradient may plateau, but this remains unverified. Conversely, the lower boundary at which phase-modulated amplification first emerges is not yet characterized."

"**No throughput evaluation.** We do not measure inference throughput or latency, which are necessary for deployment analysis but orthogonal to our severity characterization."

### Section L: Benjamini-Hochberg FDR Correction

"Table 11 compares Bonferroni (k=4, per model×strategy family) and Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction across all 44 statistical tests. BH-FDR recovers 5 additional significant results beyond Bonferroni, all in low-effect-size conditions (random eviction or cross-model random comparisons). All 32 Bonferroni-significant results remain significant under BH-FDR."

"The 5 BH-only results are: DeepSeek random s=0.25 and s=0.30 adjacent-sparsity (BH q=0.0025), DeepSeek random→0.25 → 0.30 adjacent-sparsity (BH q=0.0078, cross-model Mann-Whitney..."

**Table 11: Bonferroni vs. BH-FDR correction summary (α=0.05, 44 tests). "BH only" denotes tests significant under BH-FDR but not Bonferroni.**

| adj-s rand (k=8) | 0 | 0 |
| Adjacent sparsity (k=12) | 10 | 0 |
| Cross-model Mann-Whitney (k=4) | 7 | 2 |

(Note: some row values may be slightly off due to image resolution—the total is 32 Bonferroni-significant and 5 BH-only.)

"...random s=0.25 and s=0.30 per-condition Wilcoxon p=0.0648/0.005, BH q=0.021, DeepSeek random s=0.25 → 0.30 adjacent-sparsity (BH q=0.0078), and cross-model random...s=0.25→0.30 Mann-Whitney (p=0.0601/0.17, BH q=0.0180/0.005). All involve random eviction—the weakest effects— confirming that Bonferroni is conservative but does not miss any importance-based findings."

### Section M: Minimum Phase Length Sensitivity

"Table 12 reports the paired median difference Δ under three min_phase_length (mpl) settings across all 16 conditions (2 models × 2 strategies × 4 sparsity levels). Conclusions are robust: all importance-based conditions remain significant at p_boot < 10^-10 across mpl ∈ {5, 10, 20}; random conditions maintain the same significance pattern as significant at s < 0.20, significant at s > 0.25. Median Δ values vary by < 5% between mpl settings for DeepSeek importance, confirming that the severity gradient is not an artifact of the merging threshold."

"The main effect of increasing mpl is reduced n_eff at mpl=20: DeepSeek retains 431/500 problems and Qwen retains 289/500 (null-rate rate rises to 71.2% and 84.6%, respectively). Despite this sample reduction, all significance conclusions hold."

### Section N: Segmentation Robustness

"Table 13 reports the paired median difference Δ under tercile, quartile, and quintile segmentation for both models under importance-based eviction. Phase gradient direction and statistical significance are preserved under quartile and quintile segmentation (n=50 spot check), indicating that the tercile-based findings are not an artifact of the segmentation choice."

"The quartile and quintile Δ values are comparable to or slightly larger than tercile values because finer-grained segmentation isolates more extreme..."

### Section O: Outlier Robustness Analysis

"The extreme mean/median ratio (up to 97.60:1 in individual conditions) reflects heavy-tailed H distributions driven by near-zero denominators in specific problems.
